passages.t: What the book is for, and where wisdom begins
passages.happening:
The book opens with a title: ‘These are the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel’ (verse 1).

Then one long sentence says what the proverbs are for: ‘for gaining wisdom and discipline, for comprehending words of insight’ (verse 2), for learning to live wisely, with righteousness, justice and fairness (verse 3). They will give good sense to the simple and knowledge to the young (verse 4). And the wise are not left out: ‘let the wise listen and gain instruction’ (verse 5).

Then comes the motto of the whole book: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Solomon was remembered as the king who asked God for wisdom, and who ‘composed three thousand proverbs’ (1 Kings 4:32). The heading ties the book to him, though later headings show that other sayings were added over time. These first seven verses read as a preface to the whole book, not to chapter 1 alone.

A proverb, mashal in Hebrew, sets one thing beside another so that a pattern in life becomes clear. That tells a reader how to take the book: as observations about how life usually goes under God, not as laws or guarantees.

Notice who the book is for. The simple, peti in Hebrew, are the naive and inexperienced, open like a door that anyone can walk through. They are not yet fools. They can go either way. But the book also speaks to the wise, who still have more to learn.

The fear of the LORD is not terror. It is reverence and trust toward God, shown in obedience: a sober recognition that God is God. The book calls it ‘the beginning’, the first step and the starting point. Wisdom is moral and religious before it is practical.
passages.later: Solomon's own prayer for wisdom was for ‘an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil’ (1 Kings 3:9). The psalms say the same as this motto: ‘The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom’ (Psalm 111:10). And Ecclesiastes ends where Proverbs begins: “Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
passages.asks: The book says that knowing God comes first, before skill, success or cleverness. Ask what you treat as the beginning of a good life. And ask whether you still let yourself be taught, as the book asks even of the wise.

passages.t: Do not walk the road with them
passages.happening:
Now the father speaks: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother” (verse 8). Their teaching will be like ‘a garland of grace on your head and a pendant around your neck’ (verse 9).

Then he warns his son about a gang. “My son, if sinners entice you, do not yield to them” (verse 10). He gives their pitch: come along, lie in wait for blood, ambush the innocent. ‘We will find all manner of precious goods; we will fill our houses with plunder’ (verse 13). Throw in your lot with the gang, they say, and all will share one purse.

“My son, do not walk the road with them or set foot upon their path” (verse 15). ‘For their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood’ (verse 16). But the trap they set is for themselves: ‘they lie in wait for their own blood; they ambush their own lives’ (verse 18). ‘Such is the fate of all who are greedy, whose unjust gain takes the lives of its possessors’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world wisdom was taught at home and at court, and teaching was often framed as a father speaking to his son. Egyptian teaching texts used the same form. Proverbs keeps it, and adds two things. The mother's teaching is honored beside the father's. And the goal is not only success but a life that is right before the LORD.

A garland and a pendant were marks of honor, as a medal or a wedding ring is now. What the parents teach will mark the son as someone worth trusting.

The gang's offer was real. Roads between towns had no police, and bands of robbers could ambush travelers for their goods. Their pitch is the oldest one: easy money, and a place to belong. The father answers it by following the plan to its end. The net they spread for others catches them. Greed carries its own ruin inside it.
passages.later: The psalms open the same way: ‘Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners’ (Psalm 1:1). Isaiah describes a whole people gone this way: ‘Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood’ (Isaiah 59:7). And Paul warned that ‘Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation’ (1 Timothy 6:9), and ‘the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil’ (1 Timothy 6:10).
passages.asks: The gang promised money and belonging. Ask which voices in your life promise quick gain or a place in the group if you will only go along. And ask what it would look like to follow one of those plans to its end before you take the first step.

passages.t: Wisdom cries out in the street
passages.happening:
‘Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square’ (verse 20). She cries out in the busiest places of the city, at the city gates.

“How long, O simple ones, will you love your simple ways? How long will scoffers delight in their scorn and fools hate knowledge?” (verse 22). If they had turned at her rebuke, she would have poured out her spirit on them and made her words known (verse 23).

But they refused her call, and ‘no one took my outstretched hand’ (verse 24). So when trouble comes like a storm, she will not answer them. ‘Then they will call on me, but I will not answer; they will earnestly seek me, but will not find me’ (verse 28). ‘So they will eat the fruit of their own way’ (verse 31).

She ends with a promise: “But whoever listens to me will dwell in safety, secure from the fear of evil” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Wisdom is pictured as a woman, a way Hebrew poetry has of giving a quality a voice so that it becomes vivid and personal. To choose wisdom is to answer someone who calls, not only to learn a set of rules.

Notice where she speaks. The street, the square and the city gate were the busiest places in an ancient town. At the gate the elders heard legal cases, merchants traded, and news passed from mouth to mouth. Wisdom is not hidden in a temple or a school. She speaks where ordinary business happens, and she speaks loudly.

Her speech sounds like a prophet's: a call, a charge, a warning of judgment and a promise. The chapter brings in three of the book's characters: the simple, who are naive; the scoffer, who mocks correction; and the fool, who is settled in folly.
passages.later: Isaiah heard God speak of the same outstretched hands: ‘All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people’ (Isaiah 65:2), words Paul quotes in Romans 10:21. And Paul states the law Wisdom describes in verse 31: ‘Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return’ (Galatians 6:7).
passages.hard:
Does Wisdom really laugh at people's disasters and refuse to answer when they finally call?

Verses 26 to 28 are hard to read. Wisdom says she will mock the calamity of those who refused her, and will not answer when they seek her.

Two things help. First, this is poetry in the style of a prophet's warning, and its point is how serious the choice is. There comes a point when the results of years of foolish choices arrive and cannot be undone. Someone who has scorned good counsel for years cannot summon wisdom in a moment of crisis. Her mocking also turns back on the scoffers their own scorn (verse 22).

Second, the speech is spoken now, while there is still time. It is addressed to those who keep on refusing, and its purpose is to turn the hearer before the storm comes. Her outstretched hand (verse 24) shows the invitation was real. The rest of Scripture shows God welcoming everyone who turns back, and it also warns that putting it off is dangerous.

And verse 33 describes the usual fruit of listening, a life of safety, as a pattern under God. It is not a promise that the wise never suffer. That is a question the books of Job and Ecclesiastes take up directly.
passages.asks: Wisdom speaks in the busiest places. Ask where in an ordinary day she might be calling to you, if you were listening. And ask whether there is counsel you have been putting off, and what it would mean to take her hand today.
